meta.title: AI tools across review stages
meta.snapshotQualification: RAISE 3 v4 p. 3 calls Table 2 a September 2026 snapshot; the p. 12 caption still says February 2026. This map identifies the exact document version rather than treating the table as a live product catalogue.
meta.licence: RAISE sources: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International; this guide is an independent adaptation.

recommendations.label: Acceptable for use
recommendations.description: Outputs may be used directly when their limitations and potential biases are acknowledged and addressed.

recommendations.label: Human verification required
recommendations.description: A human must carefully check outputs before use—typically the entire output—and correct them as needed. Fluent or plausible wording does not demonstrate accuracy.

recommendations.label: Requires validation within the review
recommendations.description: Test the intended task and workflow within this review against a task-specific threshold set in advance and an appropriate benchmark. The workflow must meet that standard; previous use elsewhere or convincing examples are insufficient.

recommendations.label: Exploratory and supplementary use
recommendations.description: Use outputs to develop ideas, with extensive human refinement before using them in a review, or to supplement established processes without replacing them.

recommendations.label: Not acceptable for use
recommendations.description: Outputs have serious limitations for the specified use and should not be relied upon.

functions.descriptionMd: ASySD identifies repeated bibliographic records in search results, allowing a review to retain a single record rather than screen the same publication repeatedly. Its developers provide both an R package and a web application.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes deduplication as comparing bibliographic details using prescribed similarity criteria. The [ASySD development and evaluation paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10483700/) explains how the tool cleans these details, finds potential matches and applies string comparisons and decision rules to identify duplicates. These defined matching procedures explain its rule-based classification.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats deduplication as a mature application: many validated tools have low rates of incorrectly identifying distinct records as duplicates. However, matching rules can be specific to a domain, so suitability still depends on the records in the review. Assess that fit and retain an audit trail of duplicate pairs where possible. The recommendation applies to this type of function; it does not guarantee error-free ASySD performance in every review.
functions.officialUrlMd: [ASySD developer repository](https://github.com/camaradesuk/ASySD), which links its R package documentation and Shiny application.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6.

functions.descriptionMd: GRADE-CERQual supports assessment of confidence in findings from a qualitative evidence synthesis. It is an assessment framework, not a standalone AI program. The official site distinguishes it from iSoQ, the online platform that helps authors apply the framework.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Table 2 groups GRADE-CERQual with template-based resources that support established assessment frameworks. The rule-based classification refers to this structured application of criteria. Reviewers use the framework to assess confidence; it does not read all the studies and make that judgement autonomously.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explicitly requires humans to retain certainty judgements. Interpretation: a structured template can help reviewers organise and document how they apply the criteria, while they remain responsible for assessing the findings. This explains the acceptable recommendation for framework support; it is neither approval of automated confidence judgements nor a claim that CERQual itself is AI software.
functions.officialUrlMd: [GRADE-CERQual](https://www.cerqual.org/). The coordinating team's site separately links the [iSoQ application](https://isoq.epistemonikos.org/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: CINeMA helps reviewers assess confidence in network meta-analysis findings. Its official documentation describes a framework covering within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity and incoherence. A contribution matrix shows how individual studies inform the network estimates.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE groups CINeMA with tools that implement established certainty-assessment frameworks. Prespecified calculations and structured displays organise the information reviewers need to assess confidence. This support for human assessment is the rule-based function represented here; the final certainty rating remains a reviewer judgement.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE's condition is that humans still make certainty judgements. Interpretation: CINeMA helps reviewers inspect the inputs and follow a structured assessment process, but they must evaluate the concerns and justify the resulting confidence rating. The acceptable recommendation therefore concerns this assistance, not an unattended process that turns raw studies into recommendations.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CINeMA](https://cinema.med.auth.gr/). The [University of Bern development repository](https://github.com/esm-ispm-unibe-ch/cinema) documents the application.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: citationchaser retrieves a known paper's references and papers that cite it, helping reviewers discover potentially eligible studies beyond the main keyword search. Its official implementation describes these as backward and forward searches of bibliographic citation data.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The tool follows recorded citation relationships through database software interfaces (APIs), using a defined retrieval procedure. Those explicit links and instructions explain the rule-based classification. Reviewers then decide whether the retrieved papers are eligible.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE considers citation chasing useful when weak keyword indexing causes searches to miss studies. Its usefulness depends on the citation database's coverage, and it can favour older or heavily cited work. Interpretation: use it as an additional search route, document the starting papers and data sources, and assess the retrieved evidence. The extra route broadens discovery but still requires reviewer screening and search documentation.
functions.officialUrlMd: [citationchaser developer repository](https://github.com/nealhaddaway/citationchaser), linking the [web application named in RAISE](https://estech.shinyapps.io/citationchaser/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: In RAISE's listed use, CiteSource helps check whether search results contain articles from a reference set used as a benchmark. Its documentation describes retaining information about each record's source and search string when records are merged, so reviewers can compare what different searches contribute.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This function uses record matching, identifiers, deduplication and counts to compare retrieved records with a specified reference set. These defined operations show which benchmark articles a search found, giving reviewers an inspectable check of its coverage.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Table 2 describes the matching workflow but gives no separate CiteSource-specific rationale. Interpretation: the comparison is useful because it provides a transparent check against known articles. Its value depends on the benchmark: finding every article in a small or biased set does not establish that all relevant literature was retrieved. Reviewers must therefore judge both the reference set and the search strategy.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14 (query validation). The benchmark-quality limitation is editorial interpretation of the reference-set check.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE lists Connected Papers under citation chasing: starting with a known paper to find related literature beyond the original keyword search. The official explanation clarifies how its graph works: papers are connected by co-citation (being cited together) and bibliographic coupling (sharing references). A connection therefore indicates similarity, not necessarily that one paper directly cites the other.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this search function in its rule-based category. Interpretation: the tool uses citation relationships and a specified graph-similarity procedure to find related papers. This explains the mapped function, but does not establish that every component of the current product uses only fixed rules or that every graph connection is a direct citation.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE values citation-based discovery because it can find studies missed by keyword searches. Coverage and citation bias still limit what appears in the graph, so related-paper discovery is an additional route, not evidence that retrieval is comprehensive. Reviewers must still screen the candidates.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: These applications support quantitative meta-analysis. The official CRSU site describes R Shiny interfaces for statistical synthesis, visualisation and sensitivity analysis; the name covers a suite of applications rather than one algorithm.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes these applications as running underlying R or Python calculations on effect estimates and summary statistics, with parameters chosen by the user. Established statistical models determine how the results are pooled. This execution of specified analytical procedures explains the rule-based grouping.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires statistical parameters to be documented and adjustable, sound input data, and reviewers who can choose appropriate analyses. Interpretation: software can perform the calculations while reviewers retain responsibility for the method and its assumptions. The acceptable recommendation therefore does not decide whether the studies should be pooled or select the right model for the review.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CRSU meta-analysis apps, University of Glasgow](https://www.gla.ac.uk/research/az/crsu/apps/). The verified official suite uses **CRSU**.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: Deduklick identifies duplicate records in bibliographic search results. The developer describes it as a dedicated automated deduplication product; this entry covers only that Table 2 function.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this deduplication function in its rule-based category. The [published 2022 implementation](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-022-02045-9) describes natural language processing (NLP) to prepare the records, standardisation of bibliographic details, similarity comparisons and expert-derived matching rules. These procedures explain the specific function shown here; the paper is not a complete audit of every component in the current proprietary product.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE considers validated deduplication approaches mature, but warns that matching rules developed for one domain may not generalise. Interpretation: check the product's evidence and whether the review's records suit its approach, retaining transparent duplicate decisions where possible. The recommendation supports this function without substantiating vendor performance claims for every dataset.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6. The mechanism description is additionally supported by Borissov and colleagues’ 2022 methods paper, linked above.

functions.descriptionMd: Display a review's coded evidence as an interactive evidence-and-gap map. The official documentation describes exporting coded data from EPPI-Reviewer and configuring its presentation in EPPI-Mapper. The display helps readers inspect where evidence is concentrated or sparse.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Table 2 calls this “rule-based software.” Interpretation: supplied structured data and display settings determine the visual arrangement. Reviewers provide the coding and interpret the resulting map; the software does not independently decide what a gap means or derive a cross-study conclusion.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explicitly includes visualisations of study characteristics, such as evidence-and-gap maps. Interpretation: this is a checkable presentation task, because the display can be compared with the reviewer-generated coding behind it. Reviewers remain responsible for that coding, the map dimensions, filters and interpretation. An empty cell shows a gap in the displayed data; it does not by itself establish that no relevant research exists.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17 (visual synthesis). The explanation of checkable rendering and the caution about empty cells are editorial interpretation of that row.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE lists the platform as an interface for bringing bibliographic records into a review. The official help describes importing common reference formats and importing results of a PubMed search run from within EPPI-Reviewer.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This entry covers a defined procedure for retrieving and importing records. RAISE distinguishes functions within multipurpose platforms, so this classification applies to EPPI-Reviewer's record-transfer function. Its classifiers and generative features have to be considered separately, even though they share the platform name.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE recognises retrieval through review platforms, while noting that not every database is accessible through a software interface (API). Interpretation: a specified query and documented import route can make retrieval transparent, provided reviewers check database coverage, access and successful transfer. Importing citation records does not ensure that all full texts are available or that the overall search is complete.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: EviAtlas displays datasets produced by systematic maps, including geographical evidence displays. The official project describes using previously assembled and coded evidence to help readers explore and understand its distribution.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE calls this function “rule-based software.” Interpretation: structured records, geographic fields and user settings determine the display. The software presents the evidence in those records; reviewers interpret what the body of evidence means.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explicitly includes visualisations of study characteristics, such as evidence-and-gap maps. Interpretation: the display can be checked against the reviewer-generated coding behind it. Reviewers remain responsible for that coding, the map dimensions, filters and interpretation. An empty cell shows a gap in the displayed data; it does not by itself establish that no relevant research exists.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17 (visual synthesis). The explanation of checkable rendering and the caution about empty cells are editorial interpretation of that row.

functions.descriptionMd: GRADEpro helps reviewers apply and document an established certainty-assessment framework. Its official platform describes structured assessments, evidence tables and associated calculations.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places this template-supported assessment function in its rule-based category. Structured fields and predefined calculations and displays help reviewers record their assessments. This classification concerns that function; other features of the platform need separate consideration.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE's explicit condition is that humans still make certainty judgements. Interpretation: standardised recording can help reviewers apply and report the framework consistently, while they assess the evidence and justify each rating. A completed template cannot establish that those judgements are sound, and the recommendation does not extend to automated certainty assessment across all platform functions.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (template support; humans retain certainty judgements). General certainty-assessment background, p. 9; product-specific details are attributed to the linked official resources.

functions.descriptionMd: The meta R package provides standard meta-analysis models and associated plots. RAISE lists it as an example of software that performs specified statistical analyses on supplied data.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The package runs defined statistical procedures using the data and parameters selected by the user. RAISE's rule-based category includes this conventional statistical programming: the specified model governs the calculation.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires documented, adjustable parameters, sound input data and sufficient analytical knowledge. Interpretation: reproducible calculations support a defensible synthesis when reviewers choose appropriate effect measures and models. They must also judge whether pooling is meaningful and interpret heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses; the software does not take over those decisions.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: The developer's documentation describes R functions for effect-size calculation, fitting meta-analytic models, moderator/meta-regression analysis and plots. This entry represents RAISE's statistical-analysis use rather than every possible package operation.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The supplied data, chosen model and statistical routines determine the calculations. RAISE's broad rule-based category includes this conventional statistical software. The package executes an analysis; reviewers develop and justify the evidence-synthesis argument.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE requires transparent, adjustable statistical parameters and human analytical expertise. Interpretation: code and outputs that can be inspected support accountability, but even a correctly executed analysis can answer an inappropriate question or combine studies invalidly. Reviewers remain responsible for preparing the data, handling relationships between estimates, checking assumptions, choosing the model and interpreting the results.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 17; supporting discussion, pp. 8–9.

functions.descriptionMd: The platform can execute searches through supported database software interfaces (APIs) and import bibliographic search files; these are ways to bring records into a review workspace. These details are described in its official documentation.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This entry covers a defined procedure for executing searches and transferring records. That explains its rule-based classification. The separately listed Smart Search feature has an agentic classification, and other AI features also require separate consideration; this category describes the citation-retrieval function, not the entire platform.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE recognises automated retrieval through review platforms, but notes that database software interfaces (APIs) are not universally available. Interpretation: documenting the database, query, date and transfer route makes the process traceable. Reviewers must also check access restrictions and verify that expected records were imported. The recommendation does not establish coverage of every database, full-text access or a comprehensive overall search.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: PredicTER estimates the time and resources needed for a review from user-supplied parameters. The estimate helps the team plan the work; it does not carry out review tasks.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places PredicTER in the rule-based class. The developer describes an algorithm that combines expected evidence volumes and working speeds, with assumptions the user can edit. The estimate follows this structured calculation.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE lists resource estimation as acceptable. Interpretation: reviewers can inspect and adjust the assumptions to inform their plan, while retaining responsibility for its feasibility. Defaults reflect the contexts from which they were derived, so the estimate is neither a guaranteed completion time nor evidence that an under-resourced review can be delivered.
functions.officialUrlMd: [PredicTER — official tool and methods](https://predicter.github.io/). The developer explains that default evidence volumes and working speeds came from environmental reviews and a survey of experienced reviewers, and can be tailored.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 12. The mechanism/default-context explanation is from the linked official tool page; the planning caveat is source-aligned interpretation.

functions.descriptionMd: The application analyses PubMed results and produces frequency tables, including words used in titles/abstracts and indexing information. Reviewers can use these patterns to identify candidate search terms.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The tool counts and tabulates terms from a specified set of PubMed records. This defined text-analysis procedure shows the language present in that sample, giving reviewers candidate terms to consider when developing the search.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats term-frequency analysis as a complement to other search-development methods and specialist expertise. Interpretation: patterns in the initial results can reveal useful terms, but also reflect that sample's omissions and biases. Reviewers must therefore assess the suggestions and adapt the search to each database; a PubMed-based analysis cannot establish adequate sensitivity or resolve all indexing differences.
functions.officialUrlMd: [PubReMiner, Amsterdam UMC/AMC](https://hgserver2.amc.nl/cgi-bin/miner/miner2.cgi), the application linked in RAISE.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE lists ResearchRabbit under citation chasing: exploring literature connected to known papers to find additional candidates. Its current official site describes interactive maps of papers, authors and concepts, alongside an adaptive recommendation engine.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The rule-based label follows RAISE's classification of this citation-chasing function. However, the developer describes algorithms that learn from user activity. The label therefore represents the function as grouped in RAISE's September 2026 v4 guidance, rather than a complete account of the current product's architecture.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE considers citation-linked discovery useful for finding studies missed by keyword searches, but notes limits from database coverage and bias towards older or frequently cited work. Interpretation: document it as an additional discovery route and screen the candidates it returns. Personalised recommendations do not establish that all relevant studies have been found.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, pp. 13–14 (citation-chasing rationale and example-list continuation). General study-identification background, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: The developers describe finding overrepresented terms in a set of relevant references so that information specialists can incorporate them into Boolean searches (which combine terms using operators such as AND and OR). The application supports text analysis of free-text terms and controlled vocabulary (standardised indexing terms).
functions.whyCategoryMd: The tool applies defined quantitative text-analysis procedures to a supplied set of references. These procedures identify candidate search terms for reviewers to assess; the reviewer then develops and tests the complete search strategy.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE permits term-frequency support alongside other search-development methods. Interpretation: the output can reveal relevant terminology, but its usefulness depends on the reference sample and how the terms are used. Expert judgement is still needed to assess that sample, test the resulting search and adapt it to each database's indexing; a supplied reference set does not automatically yield an adequate strategy.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: This entry covers study selection using domain-specific dictionaries for population, intervention, comparison and outcome (PICO) concepts. RAISE names Systematic Online Living Evidence Summaries (SOLES) as an example where these dictionaries are used. People construct regular-expression rules—text-matching patterns—to identify study characteristics, particularly in full text. The cell represents this function, not every component of a SOLES workflow.
functions.whyCategoryMd: People choose the dictionary terms and matching patterns that the software applies to study reports. This makes the listed function rule-based, rather than a classifier learned from labelled examples. SOLES itself is a broader framework that can combine several technologies, not a single universal rule-based screening application.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE warns that handcrafted dictionaries cannot adapt to unfamiliar terminology. A rule set may therefore miss relevant studies when their language differs from what its authors anticipated. Interpretation: validate whether the rules recognise the review's concepts and relevant terminology before relying on them. Success in one domain does not establish suitability in another.
functions.officialUrlMd: [CAMARADES SOLES project directory](https://camaradesuk.github.io/soles-projects/), linked by the team's [systematic-review wiki](https://camarades.de/wiki-content/11-tools.html).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 15; supporting discussion, pp. 6–7.

functions.descriptionMd: RAISE names the overall TERA platform as an example of obtaining bibliographic records programmatically or through a review interface. This general platform entry is separate from the named TERA features listed in this map.
functions.whyCategoryMd: This function follows a defined procedure to retrieve and transfer records, which explains the rule-based grouping. The classification concerns that procedure; the platform's other named features may use different mechanisms and have different recommendations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE notes that not every database offers a software interface (API) for automated retrieval. Interpretation: platforms can reduce manual record handling when the underlying sources, queries and limits are known. Reviewers still need to check coverage, successful transfer and where the records came from. The recommendation does not establish unrestricted database access, automatic full-text availability or completeness of the search.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; API-assisted retrieval discussion, p. 4; coverage and access limitations, p. 5.

functions.descriptionMd: Identify repeated records after combining results from different searches or databases, reducing redundant screening while retaining the evidence record.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places Deduplicator in the category that compares bibliographic details using prescribed similarity criteria. Those matching instructions explain the rule-based classification of this function; other TERA functions require separate consideration.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats deduplication as mature and notes low rates of incorrectly marking distinct records as duplicates among validated tools. However, specialised matching rules may not generalise to other records. Interpretation: check whether the matching suits the input data, consider the consequences of deleting a genuinely distinct report, and retain duplicate-pair evidence where available. The recommendation does not make every proposed duplicate safe to accept regardless of context.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 5–6.

functions.descriptionMd: TERA Polyglot adapts an existing search to another database's command syntax. It translates how the search is expressed, not the language of study reports or the suitability of the search concepts. RAISE 2 notes that syntax translators do not translate controlled vocabularies—standardised indexing terms such as MeSH or CINAHL headings—so these must be selected and checked separately.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE places Polyglot in its rule-based query-translation category. Interpretation: predefined conversions between search conventions automate repetitive syntax changes. Reviewers still need to understand each database's indexing and search behaviour to assess the translated strategy.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE identifies vulnerabilities from changing database interfaces, uneven maintenance and validation, and limited coverage of specialist databases. A translated query may therefore contain unsupported or outdated syntax. Reviewers must check the complete query, correct these problems and establish that its intended concepts and retrieval behaviour are preserved. This need to verify the translation explains its stronger checking requirement than generally acceptable rule-based search functions.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA Polyglot](https://tera-tools.com/polyglot), the application linked in RAISE, and the [official help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5. RAISE 2 v4 (25 August 2026), p. 17 describes the controlled-vocabulary limitation.

functions.descriptionMd: TERA Review Wizard helps structure and draft a review's methods section using supplied information and a template. RAISE lists this structured-reporting function under “Text Generation”; this map places it under “Writing a manuscript”. The function supports reporting rather than autonomous interpretation of review results.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes a template tool with a predefined reporting structure. Interpretation: standardised fields and prepared text structures organise information supplied by the review team. This structured use of the team's information explains the rule-based grouping.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE specifies the structured-reporting role but gives little additional justification. Interpretation: reviewers can inspect a template and supply the actual methods and findings, making it useful for reporting their work. They must ensure that the text accurately describes the review. The acceptable recommendation covers templating, not invented methods, synthesis or conclusions.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature. A [researcher’s TERA training presentation](https://www.ebm-netzwerk.de/de/medien/pdf/ebm2025-k-02-02-thomas.pdf) identifies methods-section drafting as the specific role.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 18 (rule-based structured reporting). The methods-section specificity comes from the separately linked TERA training presentation; the accountability caveat is editorial interpretation.

functions.descriptionMd: In RAISE's listed use, search results are compared with a reference set of articles to check coverage. Record matching, deduplication and unique identifiers help determine which reference articles the search retrieved.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The function compares specified records and identifies or counts matches. Interpretation: these defined comparisons make the benchmark check reproducible and show reviewers which articles were found.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Table 2 describes the operation but gives no separate product-specific justification. Interpretation: comparing results with known articles provides concrete evidence about a query's behaviour, but only within that reference set. Finding them all does not establish complete retrieval beyond it. Information specialists must still assess the concepts and database syntax, and check whether refinements remove genuinely relevant studies.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA official tool/help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/), which lists the named feature.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 14 (query validation). The benchmark-quality limitation is editorial interpretation of the reference-set check.

functions.descriptionMd: TERA WordFreq supports search development by counting terms in preliminary search results. Reviewers can use recurring words to identify terminology that may expand or refine the strategy.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes counting keywords and/or controlled-vocabulary terms—standardised indexing terms. These explicit counts show which language appears in the supplied records, giving reviewers a basis for considering candidate search terms.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE says frequency tools should complement other development methods and information-specialist expertise. Interpretation: frequent terms can be useful, but a rare, essential synonym may be absent from the sample. Reviewers must therefore consider the initial records and database indexing when selecting terms; frequency alone should not determine the final search.
functions.officialUrlMd: [TERA WordFreq](https://tera-tools.com/word-freq), the application linked in RAISE. The feature is also listed in the [official help directory](https://tera-tools.com/help/).
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: The application retrieves metadata for supplied PubMed identifiers and arranges indexing terms in a comparison grid. The official help explains that reviewers can inspect Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), variants and indexing differences to understand why known articles were retrieved or missed.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The application retrieves, sorts and displays existing bibliographic details using a specified procedure. RAISE groups it with keyword and controlled-vocabulary analysis. The resulting grid helps reviewers inspect term patterns and indexing differences when developing a search.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE treats these tools as complements to other search-development approaches. Interpretation: the grid makes indexing information easier to inspect, while reviewers select suitable articles, assess useful terms and adapt the strategy to each database. A MeSH-based comparison cannot establish that indexing is consistent or that concepts absent from the sample have been covered.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 13; supporting discussion, pp. 4–5.

functions.descriptionMd: Groups supplied literature into topics so reviewers can identify themes and areas of interest while developing a protocol.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Carrot2 finds patterns in supplied text without first needing examples labelled by reviewers, so RAISE places this function in **Unsupervised** learning. It groups related documents and labels the groups to make the collection easier to explore. Those groupings do not decide which studies are eligible or provide an evidence-based answer to the review question.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE lists topic exploration during protocol development as acceptable. **Interpretation:** the clusters help the team become familiar with the literature while leaving the review question and protocol decisions with the reviewers. They should account for limitations and potential biases in the groupings and still plan comprehensive searching. The recommendation does not validate every cluster or make the output an automated evidence synthesis.
functions.officialUrlMd: [Carrot2 search-results clustering](https://search.carrot2.org/). [Developer documentation/source](https://github.com/carrot2/carrot2) confirms that it groups related documents and labels the groups. The search interface requires JavaScript.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 12; technology classes, p. 3. RAISE 2 v4 (25 August 2026), p. 6 explains unsupervised learning and topic modelling.

functions.descriptionMd: Groups search results or other supplied documents into topic clusters, helping a reviewer recognise themes, terminology and possible areas of interest.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Carrot2 finds patterns in supplied text without first needing examples labelled by reviewers, so RAISE places this function in **Unsupervised** learning. It groups related documents and labels the groups to make the collection easier to explore. Those groupings do not decide which studies are eligible or provide an evidence-based answer to the review question.

functions.descriptionMd: Builds or applies a model that assigns records a category or relevance score. A bespoke model can learn from examples that reviewers have assigned to two categories; the team then decides how to use its predictions in study selection.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model learns how labelled text relates to a category or score and applies that learning to new records. This makes it supervised learning. The entry concerns using the prediction model for study selection, rather than continually changing the order of a human screening queue.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explains that training and validation data determine performance, and more complex concepts may need a wider range of examples. Even a well-developed model can be unsuitable for a different research domain or type of record: training on titles and abstracts, for example, does not automatically support use on other material. Reviewers must therefore validate the model for the intended review context. This recommendation does not give every EPPI-Reviewer model—including separately evaluated pre-built classifiers—the same performance claim.

functions.descriptionMd: Identifies reporting of items such as random allocation, blinded outcome assessment, animal exclusions, conflicts of interest and animal-welfare compliance. Reporting a safeguard does not establish low overall risk of bias.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Pre-ROB uses trained neural models to predict whether individual reporting items are present. Its repository lists convolutional neural networks (CNNs), attention-based models, hierarchical attention networks (HANs) and BERT approaches. These are trained prediction methods; using BERT does not by itself make a classifier a generative conversational LLM. RAISE places this function under **Reporting quality**, although the repository uses risk-of-bias terminology.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explains that performance depends heavily on the training material and research domain, while reliable reference judgements for appraisal can themselves be difficult to establish. **Interpretation:** reviewers should validate predictions for the reporting items and study domain they intend to assess. Detecting a relevant sentence shows what was reported; it does not independently establish that the safeguard was adequate or that risk of bias was low.
functions.officialUrlMd: [RAISE-linked Pre-ROB repository](https://github.com/camaradesuk/pre-rob). It describes neural models that predict reporting scores and retrieve sentences for preclinical risk-of-bias-related items.

functions.descriptionMd: Proposes assessments for selected domains of the original Cochrane risk-of-bias (RoB 1) framework and highlights supporting text to assist human appraisal. This conventional RobotReviewer function is not a validated RoB 2 assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: Trained models use trial-report text to make task-specific appraisal predictions, so RAISE assigns this use to **Supervised machine learning**. The category describes this appraisal function; it does not imply autonomous synthesis or cover every possible version and feature of RobotReviewer.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explains that performance depends strongly on the training material and research domain. Appraisal also requires judgement, and human reference assessors can disagree, so earlier evaluations do not establish accuracy in every review. **Interpretation:** reviewers should compare outputs with suitable independent assessments using the intended appraisal framework. Evidence for the original RoB 1 domains does not establish validity for RoB 2 or another instrument; Cochrane’s risk-of-bias workshop explicitly distinguishes these comparisons.

functions.descriptionMd: Marks information about populations, interventions, comparators and outcomes in trial PDFs so reviewers can locate study details.

This entry concerns identifying those details in reports, a separate task from predicting risk-of-bias assessments.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explains that extraction performance depends on the research domain and training material. **Interpretation:** reviewers should therefore validate extraction for the variables and reports in their own review. Good performance on a different task, such as risk-of-bias assessment, does not establish that the extraction is accurate.

functions.functionName: Risk of bias assessment in the RAISE table
functions.descriptionMd: Checks whether methods report safeguards such as randomisation, blinding and power analysis, providing information that can support appraisal. The current product describes reporting and integrity checks and explicitly does not claim to determine whether the science is correct. Its score should therefore not be treated as a complete independent risk-of-bias assessment.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns this use to **Supervised machine learning**, and the developer describes trained detection algorithms. The material checked does not establish how every current component is trained, so this placement should not be read as evidence that all SciScore features use one model.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE explains that appraisal performance depends strongly on the training material and research domain. **Interpretation:** reviewers must also check whether SciScore’s narrower reporting outputs answer their actual risk-of-bias question. A statement that randomisation occurred does not establish that it was adequate, so validation needs to address both detection accuracy and what conclusions can reasonably be drawn from the output.

functions.descriptionMd: Searches publications about neuroscience animal studies for experimental characteristics and reported safeguards, such as randomisation or blinding. It organises the detected information into reporting indicators.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE lists STEED as **Supervised machine learning**, and this map retains that source classification. However, STEED’s [published methods](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0311358) and linked code describe human-written text-matching rules, called regular expressions, rather than a learned classifier. Its placement follows RAISE; the documented implementation is rule-based.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE’s supervised-learning row requires validation because performance depends on training data and the review context; its neighbouring rule-based reporting row also requires local validation. For STEED’s documented rule-based implementation, the practical issue is whether text patterns work reliably with the wording and context of the review’s reports. **Interpretation:** reviewers should validate those reporting indicators before relying on them and keep their meaning limited to what was reported. A matching phrase does not establish how the experiment was actually conducted or provide a definitive appraisal.

functions.descriptionMd: Combines outputs from several components to propose evidence-quality ratings, with RobotReviewer required as part of the pipeline. This research software partially automates assessment; it does not establish that the contextual judgement required by GRADE has been automated successfully.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes supervised machine-learning tools linked in a pipeline, which is why this map retains that classification. URSE uses RobotReviewer’s learned components alongside [fixed extraction and scoring rules](https://github.com/alisson-mfc/urse/blob/main/server/controllers/comparators.py). It is therefore a hybrid system: learned predictions contribute to the process, but a single trained classifier does not assign the final certainty rating.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE describes URSE as proof-of-concept and says such tools cannot be used independently without stringent manual checking, which limits their efficiency gains. Its linked evaluation concerns an adaptation of GRADE, and the authors themselves do not support full automation. **Interpretation:** reviewers may use URSE to explore an assessment or add a checked supplementary output while retaining established human certainty assessment. That is why this use remains exploratory and supplementary, rather than receiving the within-review-validation recommendation given to many classifier uses.
functions.officialUrlMd: [URSE author repository](https://github.com/alisson-mfc/urse). The [RAISE-cited proof-of-concept article](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40194821/) identifies that repository and describes an adaptation of GRADE for reviews with meta-analyses of randomised trials.

functions.descriptionMd: Ask Asta to generate the overall conclusion from quantitative studies, taking on the work of synthesising their results.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE classifies this as generative LLM use because the language model produces the interpretation across studies. An agent may also retrieve the sources, but the function being rated here is generating the synthesis.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Plausible wording alone does not show that studies can reasonably be combined, results have been converted to comparable forms, or their weighting is appropriate. It also does not establish that uncertainty and differences between studies have been handled properly. Because these choices determine whether a synthesis is sound, RAISE advises against relying on the generated conclusion. This differs from asking an LLM to draft analysis code that a knowledgeable reviewer checks.

functions.descriptionMd: Ask Asta to generate an integrated conclusion across studies, taking on the researcher’s substantive qualitative synthesis.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE classifies this as generative LLM use because the language model produces the interpretation across studies. An agent may also retrieve the sources, but the function being rated here is generating the synthesis.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: A coherent narrative can conceal how studies were selected, how conflicting findings were reconciled and how conclusions were interpreted. RAISE therefore advises against relying on the generated narrative as the substantive synthesis. RAISE separately lists researcher-led assistance with summaries, codes or themes, subject to validation within the review. That narrower use does not make an automatically generated cross-study conclusion acceptable.

functions.descriptionMd: Use Asta Find Papers to become familiar with a topic and identify terminology and candidate papers.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE classifies this as agentic AI because the system develops, refines and carries out searches in response to a request written in ordinary language. The agent coordinates a sequence of actions to explore the topic.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: The agent’s search choices and available data sources limit what it can find, so reviewers need to guide it at each search step. RAISE therefore limits this use to learning about a topic and supplementing established work. It should not be relied on for formal evidence retrieval.

functions.descriptionMd: Use Asta Find Papers to identify additional candidate studies alongside conventional searching.

functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE judges that these systems can miss too many relevant studies to replace established search strategies or sources. Use them to find supplementary papers, with human direction and verification at each search step. Finding useful papers does not show that the search found all eligible studies.

functions.descriptionMd: Suggest candidate review questions from a topic or background information.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model uses patterns learned during training to generate question wording from the supplied topic and instructions.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Suggested questions can be irrelevant, incomplete or biased, and may repeat a review that already exists. A reviewer therefore needs to check the question’s scope, relevance and originality before the team adopts it.

functions.descriptionMd: Draft a protocol outline or text using a recognised format and supplied instructions.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates both prose and a proposed structure in response to the supplied instructions and format.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: A draft can follow a familiar protocol format while proposing unsound methods. The team must therefore inspect and correct the whole draft and confirm the methods it commits to using. Responsibility for those choices stays with the reviewers.

functions.descriptionMd: Suggest concepts, terms or a provisional database search strategy.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model generates search terms and query text from the supplied topic and instructions. This produces a proposed strategy; running the database search is a separate task.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE considers generated strategies inadequate to replace established search-development methods. Their quality depends on the prompt and target database, so use them as starting material. Develop and check that material using established methods and information-specialist input.

functions.descriptionMd: Rewrite an existing bibliographic search query using another database’s rules and notation, known as its syntax.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model draws on learned patterns of database search syntax to generate a rewritten query in response to the instructions.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Even a query that runs successfully may retrieve different evidence if the translation changes the intended concepts or relationships. RAISE therefore requires every generated translation to be checked line by line by a search specialist. Check the target database’s syntax, controlled vocabulary (standardised indexing terms), operators such as AND and OR, and field codes specifying which parts of a record are searched.

functions.descriptionMd: Apply inclusion and exclusion criteria to citations or reports and propose relevance judgements.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model uses the review criteria and study text supplied in a prompt to generate relevance judgements. This is language-model classification; dedicated screening classifiers are listed separately in the map.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Screening decisions can change with the complexity of the criteria, the prompt and the examples supplied. Test the actual screening procedure on relevant review material before relying on its decisions. A convincing explanation of an individual decision does not establish that the procedure has been validated for the review.

functions.descriptionMd: Generate proposed risk-of-bias judgements from study reports and explicit instructions.
functions.whyCategoryMd: The model uses the study report and instructions to generate an interpretive assessment of possible bias.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Incomplete or ambiguous reporting can lead the model to generate invented or overconfident judgements. Evaluate the assessment procedure in the intended review context before using its ratings. Careful prompting and human verification remain necessary; they cannot substitute for genuinely missing evidence.
functions.sourcePagesMd: RAISE 3 v4 (23 September 2026), Table 2, p. 16; supporting discussion, p. 8.

functions.descriptionMd: Translate titles, abstracts or relevant report passages so a human reviewer can decide whether a study meets the review’s eligibility criteria. DeepL provides the translation; the reviewer makes the inclusion decision.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes machine translation as **Generative and other machine learning approaches**, which allows for a mix of technologies. DeepL appears in the LLM group as a display exception, rather than a claim about every model, language or deployment. DeepL’s [official model documentation](https://support.deepl.com/hc/en-us/articles/14241705319580-About-DeepL-s-language-model) describes LLM-based infrastructure, but does not validate accuracy for a particular review task. The mapped function is translation of study text; it excludes the separate DeepL Write product and automated evidence appraisal.
functions.whyRecommendationMd:
RAISE requires human verification of machine translation because accuracy may be insufficient for complex tasks. If translated eligibility information is unclear, seek clarification rather than exclude a potentially relevant study solely on that wording.

Applying RAISE’s translation recommendation to this stage is this map’s interpretation, not a separate stage-specific RAISE rating or validation of DeepL’s performance.

functions.descriptionMd: Ask Elicit to generate the overall conclusion from quantitative studies, taking on the work of synthesising their results.

Google Translate appears in the LLM group as a display exception; this does not mean every language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google’s later feature descriptions also do not identify which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd:
RAISE’s cited translation research found accuracy limitations, with outcomes and results more problematic than simpler study-design or intervention information. Errors here could change the extracted evidence, so check outcome names, groups, time points, denominators, units and statistical quantities against a reliable interpretation of the original text. Older language-specific evaluations do not guarantee current extraction or final-review accuracy.

This map applies RAISE’s translation-verification requirement to data extraction; the stage association is an interpretation.

functions.functionName: Translation of inputs to human synthesis
functions.descriptionMd: Make source findings and contextual passages accessible to the human synthesis team. Verified translated information can inform the chosen quantitative or qualitative method; the translator does not pool effects, establish themes or decide the conclusion across studies.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes machine translation as **Generative and other machine learning approaches**, which allows for a mix of technologies. Google Translate appears in the LLM group as a display exception; this does not mean every language, mode or historical implementation uses a generative LLM. Google’s later feature descriptions also do not identify which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd:
Synthesis depends on understanding the source findings, including numerical meaning and qualitative or cultural context. A readable translation does not establish that studies are compatible, analytical inputs are correct or interpretation is valid, so verify the source meaning before using it.

This stage placement applies RAISE’s translation-verification requirement to supporting human synthesis. It is this map’s interpretation, not permission for machine-generated cross-study synthesis, which RAISE treats separately.

functions.functionName: Translation of inputs to human certainty judgement
functions.descriptionMd: Provide checked translations of study information or explanations used by humans applying GRADE or CERQual. This may reuse passages translated earlier in the review rather than introduce a separate translation operation; Google Translate does not rate certainty.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE describes machine translation as **Generative and other machine learning approaches**, which allows for a mix of technologies. Google’s later feature descriptions also do not identify which model was used in older evaluations.
functions.whyRecommendationMd:
Errors in translated outcomes, methods or context can carry through into a certainty assessment. Verify the source meaning and retain human judgement; a checked translation does not establish that a GRADE or CERQual conclusion is valid.

The recommendation remains **Human verification required** for translation. This is the most indirect of the five stage associations and is this map’s interpretation. No direct performance evidence for Google Translate judging certainty is asserted.

The live page's performance claims concern its own current benchmarks; they do not replace RAISE's September 2026 v4 evidence-synthesis recommendations or establish that a particular review has retrieved every eligible study.

functions.descriptionMd: Use Undermind to identify additional candidate studies alongside conventional searching.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE classifies this as agentic AI because the system selects and carries out actions to retrieve papers. It acts on the search task, as well as generating text.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE judges that these systems can miss too many relevant studies to replace established search strategies or sources. Use them to find supplementary papers, with human direction and verification at each search step. Finding useful papers does not show that the search found all eligible studies.

functions.descriptionMd: Recover numerical values from a figure by asking the AI feature to suggest axes or data points, then checking and correcting those suggestions.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE assigns its AI-feature entry to **Generative LLMs**. This map retains that classification, but the current model architecture is not independently confirmed here; the official-resource notes below explain that limitation.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: Incorrect axes or points can produce incorrect values, so compare the axes, selected points and recovered values with the original figure and correct the extraction. RAISE therefore requires human verification. Clearly defined figures may support useful assistance; extraction from more complex images remains a research question.

RAISE's name refers specifically to the AI-assisted component of **WebPlotDigitizer**, not all digitisation algorithms. The [official documentation](https://automeris.io/docs/) describes computer vision combined with manual inputs; the [official repository](https://github.com/automeris-io/WebPlotDigitizer/blob/master/README.md) distinguishes its closed AI Assist component. These public descriptions do not establish that every current extraction algorithm is an LLM. The displayed category is RAISE's assignment, not an independent architecture audit.

functions.functionName: Interacting with evidence synthesis data using a chatbot
functions.descriptionMd: Ask questions about existing evidence-synthesis data or documents, such as an evidence map. RAISE treats this interaction separately from the review stages.
functions.whyCategoryMd: RAISE treats **chatbot interaction** as a mode of LLM use. This recommendation concerns that feature, not all InfraNodus network-analysis functions. Gaps in a text network do not establish gaps in the research evidence.
functions.whyRecommendationMd: RAISE identifies difficulty establishing whether chatbot answers are accurate and complete, and keeping them within the supplied data. These limitations raise concerns about accuracy, safety and bias. Checking individual answers against source records can help identify errors, but does not establish that an answer is complete or confined to those data. Use the chatbot to explore the material; do not treat its answers as established synthesis findings.
